title: Regulating misinformation
abstract: Governments have responded to misleading advertising by banning it, engaging in counter-advertising and taxing and regulating the product. In this paper, we consider the welfare effects of those different responses to misinformation. While misinformation lowers consumer surplus, its effect on social welfare is ambiguous. Misleading advertising leads to over-consumption but that may be offsetting the underconsumption associated with oligopoly outputs. If all advertising is misinformation then a tax or quantity restriction on advertising maximizes welfare, and other policy interventions are inferior. If firms undertake quality improving investments that are complementary to misinformation, then combining taxes or bans on misleading advertising with other policies can increase welfare.
summary_en: Governments respond to misleading advertising in three main ways: bans, counter-advertising, and product taxes/regulation. Glaeser and Ujhelyi build a unified welfare framework comparing these approaches. Misinformation lowers consumer surplus, but its social-welfare effect is ambiguous because misleading ads can offset oligopoly under-provision. Pure misinformation is best addressed via advertising taxes or quantity restrictions; other interventions are inferior. When firms make quality investments complementary to misinformation, combining ad regulation with product-quality interventions can improve on either alone.
data_used: Theoretical model — welfare comparison across three policy instruments responding to firm misinformation in oligopoly markets.
policy_relevance: GVH (Hungarian Competition Authority) and NMHH (Media Authority) regulate misleading advertising. The paper's framework helps these agencies sequence interventions: when only misinformation is present, advertising taxes or bans are superior to broader product regulation. The argument also informs Hungary's misleading-financial-product disclosures (banking, insurance) at MNB.
